name: Marco Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead a small contact-centre shift handling water-bill and leak reports. My two-year college diploma was in office systems, and I am the person other agents call when a meter reading and a repair ticket disagree. I use the approved AI case sorter every day, but I check the street number and service notice before anyone tells a household its water is back. I am good at untangling a bad case, yet our centre pays below other agent rates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the money and work picture at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Lina works part time in a school kitchen; our grown children have their own households. We rent and have barely three weeks of expenses saved after replacing the boiler. Few other centres are close enough for my bus route, so my lead title is less useful on a job search than people think. I do not know what income would cover us if I stopped paid work.

say: I would tell agents the **crew closure number** matters more than a neat AI summary.
I would keep customers from hearing **“fixed”** before a repair is confirmed.
think: I know a **boiler bill** left us with only three weeks of expenses saved.
I cannot rely on my **lead title** to overcome a low wage and few bus-reachable centres.
do: Keep **paid leak-ticket reviews** and verify crew closure numbers against approved AI summaries.
Save **twenty each payday** only after a full paid week, adding to a repair envelope.
Visit **one nearby office** with timetable and payslip only if it posts a paid vacancy with better full-week hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about three weeks of savings even if AI changes little.
S0.quote: A tidy summary cannot fill a bucket.
fieldNote: His **lead skill** does not erase the low wage or tiny reserve.
The **twenty** is new saving conditional on a full paid week.
He checks one **bus-reachable opening** without leaving paid work on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my agents the case sorter can trim a note, but it cannot confirm that a water repair happened. I still want the crew closure number before we tell a customer to turn the tap on. A tidy summary cannot fill a bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think even the boring version leaves us exposed: one boiler bill took our savings down to three weeks. My lead role is steady today, but the low wage does not rebuild a cushion quickly. Few centres on my bus route means I cannot simply shop my title around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing leak tickets and the approved AI summaries on my paid shift. Each payday, if the full hours are paid, I would put twenty into a separate repair envelope before other small spending. If one nearby water-service office posts a paid vacancy with better full-week hours, I would take the bus timetable and current payslip there; I would not leave this wage on a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even if the software fizzles. The boiler was not an AI problem. Three weeks of savings is too little when a repair crew has not even given a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a shortened case note trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew closure number is a real reference I can ask for; I will not make it up because the sorter sounds certain. One wrong “fixed” message can leave someone at home with no water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that twenty coming out of your existing savings, and will you travel to every office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twenty goes into the envelope only after a paid full week, not from the three weeks already saved. If there is no posted vacancy, I keep the bus fare and my current shifts rather than make a trip every week.

steps.text: Verify crew closure numbers while reviewing paid leak tickets
Save twenty for repairs after each full paid week
Visit nearby office with timetable and payslip only for posted paid vacancy with better full-week hours

say: I would say **routine notices** may move to AI while conflicting water cases return to agents.
I would ask with my shift for **paid correction time** and written weekly rotas.
think: I fear my **lead hours** may shrink while the remaining cases grow harder.
I know daily sorter use cannot replace **Friday pay** with only three weeks saved.
do: Join our **four-person shift request** for paid AI-notice checking time and written weekly rotas.
Record **wrong street notices** on the approved system during paid work without customer names.
After own cuts, apply for **posted paid desk** with written weekly wages/hours covering rent/utilities after bus fare; leave when signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my paid hours, despite the group request and my sorter skill.
S1.quote: The four of us can ask together, but the request is not a rota.
fieldNote: The **four-person request** is actual shared worker action, not a technical presentation.
He uses the **approved system** during paid time and protects customer details.
His **own hours** may fall, so the group request does not make him secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say bill explanations and routine leak updates could be written by AI before an agent sees them. The difficult cases will come back to our shift with a caller who has already been told two different things. I would gather the agents to ask together for paid correction time and written weekly rotas, not a shorter queue with invisible work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think management may cut the junior seats and then treat my lead post as a button that can supervise three times as many cases. My daily use of the sorter helps me spot mistakes, but it will not guarantee my own paid hours. With three weeks saved, I cannot quietly accept a reduced rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I would have our four-person shift sign one request for paid time to check AI water notices and written weekly hours. I would keep recording every wrong street notice on the approved system during paid work, with customer details protected. If my own hours are cut, I would apply to a posted paid service-desk vacancy only if the written weekly wage and hours cover rent, utilities and bus fare; I would stay until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because my wage can shrink even if the work left over is harder. The four of us can ask together, but the request is not a rota. I still have to count Friday pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would make that request, and what exactly would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are four people including me on the shift request. I would ask for paid checking time because an unpaid evening fixing bot notices would take hours from Lina and me at home. I can show the manager actual corrected notices without sharing customer names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a higher hourly rate make you leave your current shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full week on paper, not just the hourly rate. If a posted desk job pays enough after the bus fare, I can apply while still doing paid calls; I would not resign before its written offer is signed.

steps.text: Sign four-person request for paid correction time and written weekly rotas
Record wrong street notices in approved system during paid work
Apply after own cuts: posted paid desk, written weekly wages/hours covering rent/utilities after bus fare
Keep paid calls until a suitable written offer is signed

I would explain that **pipe robots** arrive later than the screen change.
think: I expect a **large paid-hours cut** before rebuilding even one month of savings.

If 2028 paid calls end without a suitable opening, ask the **landlord** for a payment schedule before rent is late; approval uncertain.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely wage gap and a reserve below one month.
S2.quote: I cannot manufacture a paid vacancy on the bus route.
fieldNote: The **landlord schedule** is a request, not guaranteed assistance.
He expects **hours loss** despite strong skill and daily AI use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team full AGI by 2028 could handle bill disputes on our screens before we can rewrite the procedure. Robots repairing pipes around 2031 would be later; our call queue is the earlier target. I would tell Lina the wage is at risk, not tell her a clever sorter has made me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect a large cut in paid hours, maybe the whole shift, before I have rebuilt even one month of savings. The boiler took the buffer. My diploma and lead experience still count when a human service desk has an opening, but there are few nearby and I cannot afford an unpaid hunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week in 2026 I would put our rent, utilities, food and bus fares beside the last four payslips. If the centre ends my paid hours after 2028, I would apply for posted paid water-office or building-service work only where written weekly wage and hours cover those costs after travel. I would keep paid calls until a suitable offer is signed; if there is no opening, Lina and I would ask the landlord about a payment schedule before rent is late, without assuming it will be granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, not because I dislike AI but because the gap between a lost shift and a signed job could empty three weeks of money. I can make calls and use my diploma. I cannot manufacture a paid vacancy on the bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on the landlord giving you more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask about a schedule only if the paid calls end and no suitable job is open. I would not call it support we already have; the landlord might say no. I would bring the actual bill and proposed dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a new job financially real rather than merely promising?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An offer needs a written full-week wage and hours, not the word “competitive” in an advert. I would check the bus times and total fares before I sign or leave my current paid shift. An unpaid trial would make the gap worse, so I would not accept one.

Apply after 2028 paid-call end: posted paid work, written weekly wages/hours covering rent/utilities/food after fare
Keep paid calls until a suitable written offer is signed
Ask landlord before rent late if 2028 paid calls end without suitable opening

say: I would document **wrong bill corrections** needing human account authority.
I would say **2034 pipe robots** do not protect headset jobs from 2031 screen changes.
think: I want **charge-reversal authority**, not a forwarding title.
I know **three weeks saved** still leaves us exposed during a five-year warning.
do: Apply for the **posted paid complaint role** only with written weekly wages/hours covering rent/utilities after fare.
Take its **required account course** only with employer-paid fees and paid attendance after securing the paid opening.
Keep **paid shifts** until signed; after complaint-role failure or 2031 cuts, seek posted paid desks with written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about paid hours falling before a suitable complaint opening appears.
S3.quote: I want a paid path with a wage, not a decorative certificate.
fieldNote: The **course is required** only for a posted paid role, with fees and attendance time separately covered.
He seeks **charge authority**, not a cosmetic title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is time to document which water complaints still need a person with authority to correct a bill. The screen side could change by 2031; pipe robots follow around 2034. I would not pretend the later robot date protects our headset jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my best chance is a service-complaint role where I can actually reverse a wrong charge, not a desk that only forwards messages. Five years could let me find an opening, but three weeks of savings still leaves us vulnerable now. I want a paid path with a wage, not a decorative certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in 2026 I would ask the water office whether its posted paid complaint-officer opening requires its two-week account course, and I would apply if the written weekly wage and hours cover rent, utilities and bus fare. If I get that paid opening and the employer covers both course fees and paid hours to attend, I would take the required course and practise correcting disputed meter entries. Until a suitable signed offer, I would keep the centre’s paid lead shifts; if my hours fall around 2031, I would widen the search to posted paid building-service desks with the same full-week cost test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours falling before a complaint post opens. The longer warning gives me room to ask what the job actually requires. It does not put money in the repair envelope this Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the two-week course before a job offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not pay the account-course fee or attend without paid time just to collect paper. The training is only part of a posted paid opening that requires it, with employer-covered fees and paid attendance. My current diploma does not grant me the water office’s account authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if that specific complaint opening does not come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the complaint opening does not come, I would keep checking posted paid building-service desks. I would compare the written complete week with rent, utilities and fare, then leave only after a suitable offer is signed. The bus has to run for the shift hours.

Take required account course only after paid opening, employer-paid fees and paid attendance
Keep paid lead shifts until a suitable offer is signed
Search posted paid desks on complaint failure/2031 cuts: written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare, shift buses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years lets us count real wages and bills instead of naming a retirement date. Thinking AI could change the centre by 2036, while pipe robots would be nearer 2039. I would use the lead desk while it still pays, but I would not treat a calendar as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I hope to leave night escalations before my voice gives out, yet I have only three weeks saved. Lina’s kitchen shifts are part time and our grown children owe us no wage. I do not know what retirement income, if any, will actually be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I would compare our actual wages, rent, utilities and bus fares every three months and check any retirement income only when documented. I would keep my paid lead shifts and add twenty to the repair envelope after each full paid week. If the centre cuts hours after 2036 and we still need my wage, I would apply for posted paid service desks only where written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after travel; I would leave on a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money even with ten years to plan. The deadline is distant, but the boiler has already left us almost empty. I can make a patient plan without pretending we have a funded retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you fix a retirement date now because the warning is longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not set a stop-work date until the documented income and the bill totals actually fit. If they do not, I keep earning and revise the plan. The calendar cannot sign a rent cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the repair-envelope saving keep going after a shorter rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The twenty depends on a full paid week; I will not call our existing three weeks a new contribution. If paid hours shrink, the application needs to meet the full-week rent-and-utilities test after bus fare. My lead badge does not change that arithmetic.

steps.text: Compare actual wages, rent, utilities, fare and documented retirement income quarterly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the centre could end a paid shift before another bus-reachable vacancy is open. Three weeks saved will not carry rent and utilities through a long search. Written hours and dates from the centre, and a posted paid opening with a full-week wage after fare, would let me decide with Lina.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how often the water system says a crew has closed a leak when the household still has a dry tap. My lead badge does not repair a dry tap; a person has to call the crew and correct the notice.

headlineQuote: My lead badge does not repair a dry tap; a person has to call the crew and correct the notice.
portrait: At **58**, Marco leads water-service calls with a two-year diploma and top skill, but his wage is low.
He and Lina rent with **three weeks saved** after a boiler replacement; few centres fit his bus route.
He uses **approved AI daily** while checking actual crew closure records.
He seeks **paid account authority** through a posted role, with required training only if fees and time are covered.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end paid calls before a bus-reachable vacancy opens.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written shift dates** and a posted paid full-week offer covering rent and utilities after travel.
